a.explanation: Baclofen is an agonist at GABA-B (metabotropic) receptors — it does not act on the GABA-A receptor. Diazepam (benzodiazepine site), phenobarbitone (barbiturate site), ethanol and propofol all modulate GABA-A allosterically.

a.answer: Benzodiazepines and barbiturates bind at the same site on the neuron and enhance the activity of GABA.
a.explanation: This statement is FALSE: benzodiazepines and barbiturates bind at DISTINCT allosteric sites on the GABA-A receptor. BZs increase the frequency of Cl- channel opening, while barbiturates increase the duration of opening. The other statements are true: GABA opens receptor-operated Cl- channels; vigabatrin irreversibly inhibits GABA transaminase; tiagabine inhibits GABA reuptake; and diazepam can cause respiratory depression (especially IV).

Chronic heavy alcohol consumption causes alcoholic (dilated) cardiomyopathy, which leads to heart failure. Alcohol is not a recognised cause of angina, pulmonary hypertension, CNS tumours or renal impairment (it can affect the liver, heart, nervous system and pancreas).

Ethosuximide, valproate, clonazepam and lamotrigine are all established treatments for absence seizures. Clobazam is used mainly for Lennox–Gastaut syndrome and as an adjunctive antiepileptic — it is not a drug of choice for absence seizures.

Carbamazepine, phenytoin and valproic acid are first-line drugs for simple partial seizures and felbamate is also effective in partial seizures. Vigabatrin is not used as a first-line agent for simple partial seizures — it is reserved as adjunctive therapy for refractory partial seizures and is the drug of choice for infantile spasms (West syndrome); it can also worsen myoclonic and absence seizures.

a.answer: Insert a tongue depressor to prevent the patient from biting the tongue
a.explanation: Inserting anything (tongue depressor, spoon, fingers) into the mouth of a seizing patient is dangerous — it can cause broken teeth, injury to the patient/helper and aspiration. Turning the head to the side (to drain secretions), easing the patient to the floor, loosening restrictive clothing and calling for help if the seizure persists are all correct first-aid measures.

a.answer: Dosage of the antiepileptic drug should be adjusted to optimize seizure control regardless of the side effects
a.explanation: This is NOT a principle of AED therapy — dosage is titrated to achieve the best balance between seizure control and adverse effects. Correct principles include: proper diagnosis before drug selection, monotherapy whenever possible (eliminating polypharmacy), adding a second drug only if the first fails at optimum dose, and monitoring the pharmacokinetic profile during titration.

a.answer: Reducing Ca2+ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum in the muscle fibre
a.explanation: Dantrolene is a directly acting muscle relaxant: it inhibits ryanodine receptors, reducing Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and uncoupling excitation–contraction coupling in skeletal muscle. It does not reduce ACh release, suppress spinal reflexes, or block muscle action potentials.

Barbiturates (phenobarbitone) most commonly impair learning, memory and behaviour in children (cognitive dulling, hyperactivity). Valproic acid, phenytoin and ethosuximide have fewer cognitive/behavioural effects by comparison.

a.answer: Capacity limited metabolism saturating at higher therapeutic concentration range
a.explanation: Phenytoin exhibits saturable (Michaelis–Menten, zero-order) metabolism: the enzymes become saturated within the therapeutic range, so small dose increases cause disproportionate rises in plasma concentration. It has no significant first-pass metabolism and is hepatically metabolised, not extrahepatically.

Ataxia, nystagmus and diplopia are dose-related CNS toxicity of phenytoin, occurring at high plasma concentrations (>20–30 µg/mL). Hirsutism and gum (gingival) hyperplasia are chronic adverse effects unrelated to peak plasma concentration.

Baclofen (GABA-B agonist) is the centrally acting muscle relaxant used to control spasticity of upper motor neuron lesions (multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy). Vecuronium and succinylcholine are neuromuscular blockers (not for spasticity), and chlorzoxazone is used for acute local muscle spasm.

Diazepam is used for status epilepticus (IV), febrile convulsions, procedural sedation (cardiac catheterisation) and generalised anxiety disorder — but it is NOT used for the long-term/ongoing treatment of generalised tonic-clonic seizures (tolerance, sedation; other AEDs are used for maintenance).

a.answer: In patients with chronic insomnia a hypnotic should be used regularly
a.explanation: Hypnotics should be used only intermittently and short-term (2–3 weeks) — regular use in chronic insomnia is incorrect (it promotes tolerance, dependence and rebound insomnia). The other statements are correct principles: intermittent use for short-term stress-related insomnia, caution in sleep apnoea (all hypnotics aggravate it), and slow-elimination hypnotics for early-morning awakening.

Sodium valproate both displaces phenytoin from plasma protein binding (raising free fraction) and inhibits its hepatic metabolism (raising total levels) — a clinically important interaction. Cimetidine and chloramphenicol inhibit metabolism but do not displace; carbamazepine induces phenytoin metabolism.

Carbamazepine is effective in manic-depressive (bipolar) illness as well as epilepsy. Valproate and lamotrigine are also mood stabilisers, but among the options (ethosuximide, primidone, phenobarbitone, carbamazepine) only carbamazepine has this dual role.

Sodium valproate has multiple mechanisms: it prolongs Na+ channel inactivation, attenuates T-type Ca2+ currents (relevant to absence seizures), and inhibits GABA transaminase while increasing GABA synthesis (GAD activity) — so all three statements (a, b and c) are correct.

Methylphenidate (a CNS stimulant that blocks dopamine/NE reuptake) is the standard pharmacotherapy for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (hyperkinesia) in children. Tyramine, cocaine, phenoxybenzamine and ephedrine are not used for this indication.

a.answer: Blocks NE (and dopamine, in the CNS) reuptake via the amine pump
a.explanation: Cocaine blocks the amine (monoamine) reuptake pump — NE reuptake in the periphery and dopamine (and NE) reuptake in the CNS — producing sympathomimetic effects (tachycardia, hypertension, vasoconstriction) and CNS stimulation/euphoria. It does not activate α2 receptors, directly activate adrenoceptors, inhibit MAO, or prevent exocytosis.

Entacapone is a peripheral COMT inhibitor that reduces the peripheral O-methylation of levodopa to 3-OMD, increasing the amount of levodopa crossing the blood–brain barrier and enhancing its central effect. Donepezil and tacrine are anticholinesterases (Alzheimer's), selegiline is a MAO-B inhibitor, and trihexyphenidyl is an anticholinergic.

b.modelAnswer:
a) Status epilepticus — drug of choice: DIAZEPAM (IV, e.g., 10 mg slow IV, repeated if needed) or lorazepam IV. Mode of action: diazepam is a benzodiazepine that binds to the benzodiazepine (ω) site on the GABA-A receptor and allosterically enhances GABA-mediated Cl- channel opening (increases the FREQUENCY of channel opening), producing hyperpolarisation and rapid anticonvulsant effect. (Phenytoin/fosphenytoin IV is the second-line drug if diazepam fails.)

b) Drug for discharge after 4 days (maintenance therapy): PHENYTOIN (or fosphenytoin; carbamazepine/valproate are alternatives depending on seizure type).

c) Side effects of phenytoin to look out for:
• Dose-related CNS toxicity: nystagmus, ataxia, diplopia, drowsiness, confusion.
• Chronic effects: gum (gingival) hyperplasia, hirsutism, acne, coarsening of facial features.
• Haematological: megaloblastic anaemia (folate deficiency).
• Metabolic: osteomalacia/rickets (vitamin D metabolism), hyperglycaemia.
• Hypersensitivity: skin rashes, Stevens–Johnson syndrome, SLE-like syndrome, lymphadenopathy.
• Teratogenicity: fetal hydantoin syndrome (cleft lip/palate, cardiac defects).

a) Target BP in a 70-year-old: <150/90 mmHg (Kenyan/JNC-style elderly target; stricter <140/90 if tolerated). In general, reduce gradually and avoid postural hypotension.

b) Antihypertensive for this patient: a drug that does NOT worsen parkinsonism and is well tolerated in the elderly — e.g., a calcium channel blocker (AMLODIPINE), an ACE inhibitor (enalapril), an ARB (losartan) or a thiazide diuretic. AVOID methyldopa and reserpine (deplete central dopamine/NE and worsen parkinsonism).

c) Drug for parkinsonism: LEVODOPA + CARBIDOPA (a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor combination) — the most effective antiparkinsonian drug.

d) Mode of action:
• Amlodipine: blocks L-type voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation → reduced peripheral resistance and blood pressure.
• Levodopa: a dopamine precursor that crosses the blood–brain barrier, where it is decarboxylated by aromatic amino acid decarboxylase to dopamine, replenishing the depleted striatal dopamine in Parkinson's disease. Carbidopa inhibits peripheral decarboxylation, increasing the amount of levodopa reaching the brain and reducing peripheral side effects.

e) Side effects to look out for:
• Amlodipine: ankle oedema, flushing, headache, dizziness, reflex tachycardia, gingival hyperplasia, postural hypotension (elderly).
• Levodopa: nausea/vomiting, postural hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias, dyskinesias (choreiform movements), motor fluctuations (wearing-off, on-off phenomenon), psychiatric effects (hallucinations, confusion, psychosis), dark discoloration of urine/sweat.

a) Drug for insomnia: ZOLPIDEM (a non-benzodiazepine hypnotic; a short/intermediate-acting benzodiazepine such as temazepam or zopiclone is an alternative).

b) Mode of action: zolpidem selectively binds the benzodiazepine-1 (BZ1/ω1) site on the GABA-A receptor, allosterically enhancing GABA-mediated Cl- influx (increased frequency of channel opening) → neuronal hyperpolarisation and sedation with minimal muscle-relaxant/anticonvulsant effects. (Benzodiazepines act at the same ω site non-selectively.)

c) Side effects to look out for:
• Drowsiness, daytime sedation, dizziness, ataxia (especially in the elderly — falls).
• Anterograde amnesia and cognitive impairment.
• Tolerance and dependence with prolonged use; rebound insomnia on withdrawal.
• Bitter/metallic taste (zopiclone), dry mouth.
• Rarely parasomnias (sleep-walking, sleep-driving), hallucinations.
• Respiratory depression in susceptible patients (COPD, sleep apnoea).

Drugs can target the GABA system in the following ways:
1. Direct GABA-A receptor agonists — e.g., MUSCIMOL (activates the GABA recognition site itself).
2. Positive allosteric modulation of GABA-A (enhance GABA action) — e.g., BENZODIAZEPINES (diazepam: increases frequency of Cl- channel opening) and BARBITURATES (phenobarbitone: increases duration of Cl- channel opening), also propofol and ethanol.
3. GABA-A receptor/channel antagonists — e.g., BICUCULLINE (competitive antagonist at the GABA recognition site), PICROTOXIN (blocks the Cl- channel).
4. GABA-B receptor agonism — e.g., BACLOFEN (metabotropic receptor; used in spasticity).
5. Inhibition of GABA metabolism — e.g., VIGABATRIN (irreversible inhibitor of GABA transaminase → ↑GABA) and sodium valproate (inhibits GABA-T at high concentrations).
6. Inhibition of GABA reuptake (GAT-1) — e.g., TIAGABINE (↑synaptic GABA).
7. Benzodiazepine antagonism — FLUMAZENIL (competitive antagonist at the BZ site; used to reverse benzodiazepine effects).

Three anticonvulsants used in bipolar disorder:
1. SODIUM VALPROATE (valproic acid) — Mode of action: multiple — use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated Na+ channels, attenuation of T-type Ca2+ currents, and enhancement of GABAergic transmission (inhibits GABA transaminase, increases GAD activity). It is a broad-spectrum mood stabiliser effective in acute mania and prophylaxis.
2. CARBAMAZEPINE — Mode of action: use-dependent blockade of voltage-gated Na+ channels (slows recovery from inactivation), reducing repetitive neuronal firing; also affects Ca2+ channels and adenosine receptors. Effective in acute mania (and its derivative oxcarbazepine) and prophylaxis, especially in rapid cyclers.
3. LAMOTRIGINE — Mode of action: blockade of voltage-gated Na+ channels and inhibition of glutamate (excitatory neurotransmitter) release. Particularly effective for the DEPRESSIVE phase of bipolar disorder and maintenance.
(Note: Lithium remains the standard mood stabiliser, but these anticonvulsants are important alternatives.)

Two examples of hallucinogens and their modes of action:
1. LSD (lysergic acid diethylamide) — a 5-HT2A (serotonin) receptor partial agonist in the cortex; activation of 5-HT2A receptors alters cortical network activity, producing perceptual distortion, hallucinations and mood changes. (Psilocybin and mescaline act similarly at 5-HT2A receptors.)
2. PHENCYCLIDINE (PCP, 'angel dust') — a non-competitive antagonist at the NMDA (glutamate) receptor (blocks the channel pore), producing dissociation, hallucinations, agitation and psychotomimetic effects. (Ketamine is a related NMDA antagonist.)
(Alternative: Cannabis/THC — partial agonist at CB1 cannabinoid receptors — can produce hallucinogenic/perceptual effects at high doses.)

Pharmacological actions of methylxanthines (caffeine, theophylline):
1. CNS stimulation — increased alertness, arousal, restlessness; high doses cause anxiety, tremors and convulsions; respiratory centre stimulation (used in apnoea of prematurity — caffeine).
2. Cardiac stimulation — positive inotropic and chronotropic effects (increased force and rate of contraction; can cause arrhythmias).
3. Smooth muscle relaxation — bronchodilation (theophylline in asthma/COPD), relaxation of biliary and other smooth muscle; uterine relaxation.
4. Vasodilation — of most vascular beds (coronary, pulmonary, peripheral) but cerebral vasoconstriction.
5. Diuresis — increased renal blood flow and inhibition of tubular Na+ reabsorption (weak diuretic).
6. Skeletal muscle stimulation — increased contractility and reduced fatigue.
7. Increased gastric acid and pepsin secretion.
8. Metabolic effects — lipolysis, glycogenolysis, increased metabolic rate.
Mechanism: non-selective phosphodiesterase inhibition (↑cAMP/cGMP), antagonism of adenosine receptors, and enhanced Ca2+ mobilisation.

c.modelAnswer:
DIAZEPAM:
a) Mode of action (2 marks):
Diazepam is a benzodiazepine that binds to the benzodiazepine (ω) allosteric site on the GABA-A receptor and enhances GABA-mediated Cl- channel opening (increases the FREQUENCY of channel opening), causing hyperpolarisation and CNS depression. It has no intrinsic GABA-mimetic activity of its own.

b) Clinical applications (5 marks):
1. Anxiety disorders — generalised anxiety disorder (short-term), panic attacks.
2. Insomnia — short-term treatment (as a hypnotic).
3. Status epilepticus — IV diazepam is first-line; also febrile convulsions.
4. Premedication and sedation — cardiac catheterisation, endoscopy, dental procedures, conscious sedation (amnesic).
5. Muscle spasm — relief of skeletal muscle spasm (e.g., tetanus, spasticity), acute back pain.
6. Alcohol withdrawal — prevention of delirium tremens and seizures.

c) Side effects (3 marks):
1. Sedation, drowsiness, ataxia, impaired psychomotor performance (falls in the elderly).
2. Anterograde amnesia, confusion, paradoxical excitement (especially children/elderly).
3. Tolerance, psychological and physical dependence; withdrawal/rebound phenomena (insomnia, anxiety, seizures) on abrupt discontinuation.
4. Respiratory depression and hypotension (mainly with IV use).

 d) Drug–drug interactions (3 marks):
1. CNS depressants — alcohol, opioids, barbiturates, antihistamines: additive CNS depression and respiratory depression.
2. CYP3A4 inhibitors — cimetidine, ketoconazole, fluoxetine: ↓diazepam metabolism → ↑levels/sedation.
3. Enzyme inducers — rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone: ↑metabolism → ↓effect.
4. Theophylline and caffeine — functionally antagonise the sedative effects.

 e) Contraindications (3 marks):
1. Acute narrow-angle glaucoma.
2. Severe respiratory insufficiency / sleep apnoea (respiratory depression).
3. Myasthenia gravis (muscle relaxant effect).
4. Severe hepatic impairment (impaired metabolism).
5. Pregnancy (first trimester — teratogenic risk; near term — neonatal depression) and breast-feeding.
6. Known hypersensitivity; CNS-depressed or comatose patients; porphyria.

f) Pharmacokinetics (4 marks):
• Absorption: well absorbed orally; also IM/IV (IV for status epilepticus).
• Distribution: highly lipid-soluble, crosses the blood–brain barrier rapidly; ~98% protein-bound; crosses placenta and enters breast milk; large Vd with accumulation in fat on repeated dosing.
• Metabolism: hepatic — CYP3A4 demethylation/hydroxylation to ACTIVE metabolites (N-desmethyldiazepam, oxazepam, temazepam), then glucuronidation; slow elimination (long half-life ~30–60 h for diazepam plus active metabolites).
• Excretion: renal (as conjugates); not significantly removed by haemodialysis.
• Kinetics: repeated dosing causes accumulation; effect correlates with plasma concentration.

Compare and contrast BACLOFEN and DANTROLENE:
a) Mode of action (4 marks):
• Baclofen: agonist at GABA-B (metabotropic) receptors in the spinal cord — increases K+ conductance and decreases Ca2+ influx, inhibiting excitatory neurotransmitter release from primary afferents and reducing monosynaptic/polysynaptic spinal reflexes → reduced muscle spasticity (acts at spinal level).
• Dantrolene: acts DIRECTLY on skeletal muscle — inhibits ryanodine receptors on the sarcoplasmic reticulum, reducing Ca2+ release and uncoupling excitation–contraction coupling → reduced muscle contraction regardless of neural input (acts peripherally, not on reflexes).

b) Clinical applications (4 marks):
• Baclofen: spasticity in multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy, stroke; intrathecal baclofen for severe spasticity; also used in trigeminal neuralgia and alcohol dependence (adjunct).
• Dantrolene: malignant hyperthermia (drug of choice), neuroleptic malignant syndrome, chronic severe spasticity (UMN lesions), serotonin syndrome (severe hyperthermia), MDMA-induced hyperthermia; also exertional heat stroke.

c) Side effects (6 marks):
• Baclofen: sedation/drowsiness, dizziness, muscle weakness, ataxia, nausea, confusion, hallucinations; abrupt withdrawal causes rebound spasticity, fever, seizures (must taper); intrathecal: hypotonia, respiratory depression.
• Dantrolene: generalised muscle weakness, drowsiness, dizziness, fatigue, diarrhoea, nausea; HEPATOTOXICITY (hepatitis — potentially fatal; risk higher in females, age >35, doses >300 mg/day); pleuritis/pericarditis with eosinophilia; (malignant hyperthermia use: phlebitis at IV site).

 d) Contraindications (3 marks):
• Baclofen: hypersensitivity; caution in epilepsy (may lower seizure threshold), psychiatric illness, peptic ulcer disease, renal impairment (dose adjustment); abrupt withdrawal contraindicated.
• Dantrolene: active hepatic disease (hepatitis/cirrhosis) — the major contraindication; pregnancy and lactation; caution in cardiac/pulmonary disease and in patients needing muscle tone for ambulation.

 e) Drug–drug interactions (3 marks):
• Baclofen: CNS depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids) — additive sedation; antihypertensives — additive hypotension; lithium and tricyclic antidepressants — caution; MAO inhibitors — enhanced hypotensive effect.
• Dantrolene: CNS depressants and other skeletal muscle relaxants — additive weakness/sedation; VERAPAMIL (and other Ca2+ channel blockers) — risk of hyperkalaemia and cardiac depression (avoid combination); oestrogens — possible increased hepatotoxicity risk; clofibrate and warfarin — increased toxicity; also enhanced neuromuscular blockade.

DRUGS USED IN MANAGEMENT OF PARKINSONISM:
a) Classes and examples (4 marks):
1. Levodopa (dopamine precursor) — always combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor: levodopa + carbidopa, levodopa + benserazide.
2. Dopamine receptor agonists — bromocriptine, cabergoline (ergot); ropinirole, pramipexole (non-ergot); apomorphine (subcutaneous).
3. MAO-B inhibitors — selegiline, rasagiline.
4. COMT inhibitors — entacapone, tolcapone.
5. Centrally acting anticholinergics — trihexyphenidyl (benzhexol), benztropine, procyclidine.
6. Amantadine — (NMDA antagonist; increases dopamine release/reduces reuptake).
7. Others — istradefylline (adenosine A2A antagonist).

b) Mode of action (6 marks):
• Levodopa: crosses the blood–brain barrier and is converted by aromatic amino acid decarboxylase to dopamine in the striatum, replenishing depleted dopamine; carbidopa inhibits peripheral decarboxylation (↑central bioavailability, ↓peripheral side effects).
• Dopamine agonists: directly stimulate postsynaptic D2 (and D1) dopamine receptors in the striatum.
• Selegiline/rasagiline: irreversibly inhibit MAO-B, reducing the metabolism of dopamine in the brain (↑dopamine availability; also neuroprotective claim).
• Entacapone: inhibits peripheral COMT, reducing the conversion of levodopa to 3-O-methyldopa → more levodopa enters the brain (used to smooth 'wearing-off').
• Anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl): block central muscarinic receptors, restoring the dopamine–acetylcholine balance in the striatum (useful in early disease, drug-induced parkinsonism).
• Amantadine: increases presynaptic dopamine release and blocks dopamine reuptake; also NMDA (glutamate) antagonism — useful for dyskinesias.

c) Side effects (6 marks):
• Levodopa: nausea/vomiting, postural hypotension, cardiac arrhythmias, dyskinesias (choreiform, peak-dose), motor fluctuations (wearing-off, on-off phenomenon), psychiatric effects (hallucinations, confusion, psychosis), dark urine/sweat, mydriasis.
• Dopamine agonists: nausea, postural hypotension, hallucinations, somnolence/sleep attacks, impulse control disorders (hypersexuality, gambling); ergot agonists — retroperitoneal/cardiac valvular fibrosis.
• Selegiline: insomnia, nausea, dizziness (MAO-A selectivity lost at high doses → cheese reaction risk).
• Entacapone: dyskinesias (enhanced levodopa effect), diarrhoea, urine discoloration, nausea.
• Anticholinergics: dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation, confusion (especially in the elderly), precipitation of glaucoma.
• Amantadine: ankle oedema, livedo reticularis, confusion, hallucinations.

d) Drug–drug interactions (4 marks):
1. Levodopa + non-selective MAO inhibitors (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) — HYPERTENSIVE CRISIS (contraindicated); selegiline (selective MAO-B) is safe at therapeutic doses but caution at high doses.
2. Levodopa + antipsychotics/metoclopramide (dopamine antagonists) — antagonise the antiparkinsonian effect.
3. Levodopa + pyridoxine (vitamin B6) — increases peripheral decarboxylation of plain levodopa, reducing effect (less relevant with carbidopa).
4. Entacapone + MAO inhibitors — additive; avoid.
5. Selegiline + pethidine (meperidine) or SSRIs — serotonin syndrome (potentially fatal).
6. Dopamine agonists + antihypertensives — additive postural hypotension.
7. Anticholinergics + other anticholinergics (TCAs, antihistamines, antipsychotics) — additive anticholinergic toxicity.
8. Amantadine + anticholinergics — additive confusion, dry mouth.
